message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation. Let me start by understanding what's going on. There are four people involved: me, my boyfriend, my roommate, and her friend. We're all living in a dorm room that has two beds and two desks. It's a pretty standard setup, I guess. The issue seems to be about the door to our room. Whenever my boyfriend and I are in our room, just hanging out, watching Netflix, or whatever, my roommate and her friend leave the door wide open. They do this on purpose, and they even laugh about it, saying "this is what you get" for showing minimal PDA (public display of affection) with my boyfriend in the room. But honestly, we're not doing anything out of the ordinary. We're just being ourselves, and I feel like we deserve some privacy. The thing is, they do this every time they leave the room, and they come back in and out multiple times an hour. Each time, I have to get up and close the door because I don't want people walking by in the dorm hallway to see us in our bed. It's uncomfortable, and I feel like they're intentionally making me feel that way. They know what they're doing, and it's really annoying. Finally, after the sixth time they leave and I have to get up to close the door, I decide to lock the door. I know my roommate has a key, so if they want to come back in, they can unlock it. But I'm tired of getting up every time they leave. It's their room, but we're all sharing it, right? So I think it's reasonable to want some privacy. Then, on their seventh trip in and out, they can't open the door because it's locked. They start banging on the door really hard, and I don't open it because I know they're just being passive-aggressive. They go back to wherever they were hanging out and get the key, come back in, and then tell me it's very rude of me to lock the door because "it's my roommate's room." I calmly explain that if they're going to make me get up and close the door every time, they can go through the hassle of unlocking it. My boyfriend also asks why they're acting so passive-aggressive for no reason. She laughs and calls me disrespectful again and leaves, leaving the door wide open. Now, I'm wondering if I'm really the asshole for just wanting my door kept closed so that everyone passing by doesn't see me in my bed. I mean, isn't that a reasonable request? We're all sharing the room, but I still deserve some privacy, right? I think about it from different angles. On one hand, it's my roommate's room, so maybe she has some say in how the door is kept. But on the other hand, we're all sharing the space, and I have a right to feel comfortable and private in my own room. It's not fair that they're intentionally making me feel uncomfortable by leaving the door open all the time. I also consider the passive-aggressive behavior they're exhibiting. They know that leaving the door open is bothering me, and they keep doing it anyway, just to get a reaction out of me. That's not mature or respectful. It's one thing to have a disagreement, but to act out in that way seems like they're not handling the situation well. Moreover, when I finally lock the door, it's not like I'm doing anything wrong. I'm just trying to maintain some privacy, which is a basic need when sharing a living space. They have the key, so if they need to come back in, they can unlock it. It's not like I'm keeping them out or anything; I'm just preventing the door from being left open, which is causing me distress. I also think about how my boyfriend is involved in this. He's supportive of me wanting privacy, and he's confused about why they're acting so passive-aggressively. It makes me feel like they're not just targeting me, but also being disrespectful to my boyfriend, which adds another layer to the situation. In the end, I feel like I'm not the asshole here. I'm just trying to maintain a sense of privacy and comfort in our shared living space. It's reasonable to want the door closed when we're in the room, especially since they're intentionally making it difficult for me. Their behavior is what's problematic, not mine.
